payload.markdown: Since I have recently built a marking language, I’m sticking with the quiz example. Quizzes need questions, so you build a Question class, giving it a mark() method. All is well until you need to support different marking mechanisms.

payload.markdown: This would serve you well, as long as marking remains the only aspect of the class that varies. Imagine, though, that you are called on to support different kinds of questions: those that are text based and those that support rich media. This presents you with a problem when it comes to incorporating these forces in one inheritance tree, as you can see in Figure 11-4.

payload.markdown: Not only have the number of classes in the hierarchy ballooned, but you also necessarily introduce repetition. Your marking logic is reproduced across each branch of the inheritance hierarchy.

payload.markdown: Whenever you find yourself repeating an algorithm across siblings in an inheritance tree (whether through subclassing or repeated conditional statements), consider abstracting these behaviors into their own type.

payload.markdown: As with all the best patterns, Strategy is simple and powerful. When classes must support multiple implementations of an interface (e.g., multiple marking mechanisms), the best approach is often to extract these implementations and place them in their own type rather than to extend the original class to handle them.

payload.markdown: Remember the Gang of Four principle, “Favor composition over inheritance”? This is an excellent example. By defining and encapsulating the marking algorithms, you reduce subclassing and increase flexibility. You can add new marking strategies at any time without the need to change the Question classes at all. All Question classes know is that they have an instance of a Marker at their disposal and that it is guaranteed by its interface to support a mark() method. The details of implementation are entirely somebody else’s problem.

items: Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Composition: Building classes from other objects instead of inheriting from them.
Inheritance: Deriving a class from a base class to reuse and specialise its behaviour.
Interfaces: A pure contract of method signatures with no implementation.
Strategy Pattern: Swapping an algorithm behind a common interface at runtime.
match: PHP 8's strict, expression form of switch that always returns a value.
Behavioral Patterns: Patterns that distribute responsibility and coordinate behaviour.

8465.title: Now it’s time to define some simple Marker objects
8465.code:
<?php
abstract class Marker
{
    public function __construct(protected string $test)

    {
        abstract public function mark(string $response): bool;
}

// listing 11.18
class MarkLogicMarker extends Marker
{
    private MarkParse $engine;

    public function __construct(string $test)
    {
        parent:: __construct($test);
        $this->engine = new MarkParse($test);
    }

    public function mark(string $response): bool
    {
        return $this->engine->evaluate($response);
    }
}

// listing 11.19
class MatchMarker extends Marker
{
    public function mark(string $response): bool
    {
        return ($this->test == $response);
    }
}

// listing 11.20
class RegexpMarker extends Marker
{
    public function mark(string $response): bool
    {
        return (preg_match("$this->test", $response) === 1);
    }
}
